q: In Hazzard's discussion of the free-radical theory of aging, which process links free-radical production to damage of cellular macromolecules?
o: Lipid peroxidation damages cellular proteins and nucleic acids
Lipid peroxidation protects cellular proteins against oxidative injury
Free-radical production reduces lipid peroxidation within aging cells
Free-radical production preserves nucleic acids by increasing caloric intake
explanation:
**Lipid peroxidation** is the main consequence of free-radical production described in this discussion (p. 1274). "The main consequence of free radical production is lipid peroxidation, which results in damage to cellular proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids." (p. 1274). The source presents increased caloric intake as a proposed driver of increased free-radical production and accelerated aging damage (p. 1274).

**A. Lipid peroxidation damages cellular proteins and nucleic acids.** Correct, this is the stated sequence: free-radical production, lipid peroxidation, and damage to proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids (p. 1274).
**B. Lipid peroxidation protects cellular proteins against oxidative injury.** Wrong, the source assigns a damaging effect to lipid peroxidation, rather than a protective effect on proteins (p. 1274).
**C. Free-radical production reduces lipid peroxidation within aging cells.** Wrong, free-radical production promotes lipid peroxidation in this account rather than reducing it (p. 1274).
**D. Free-radical production preserves nucleic acids by increasing caloric intake.** Wrong, the source links increased caloric intake to increased free-radical production and accelerated damage, rather than preservation of nucleic acids (p. 1274).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1274.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.1274

q: A 77-year-old man with chronic kidney disease and asymptomatic, non-life-threatening hyperkalemia is assessed in an outpatient clinic. Which approach addresses reversible contributors as described in Hazzard?
o: Shift potassium into cells while deferring review of contributing medications
Review contributing medications, hydration status, and reversible kidney dysfunction
Give intravenous calcium to remove the excess potassium from the body
Give sodium bicarbonate while deferring assessment of acid-base status
explanation:
**Reversible contributors** to non-life-threatening hyperkalemia include medications, poor hydration, and reversible reductions in kidney function. In asymptomatic outpatients, Hazzard recommends addressing these contributors. Calcium stabilizes the myocardial membrane without lowering potassium, while bicarbonate is described as a potassium-shifting intervention when metabolic acidosis is also present. (p. 1271)
"elimination of medications that cause hyperkalemia, improving hydration status, and addressing any reversible causes of reduction in kidney function such as medications and volume depletion." (p. 1271)
"This effect is essentially immediate, but transient, and does not lower potassium levels." (p. 1271)

**A. Shift potassium into cells while deferring review of contributing medications.** Wrong, potassium-shifting treatment does not address the contributing medications that the source specifically includes in outpatient management. (p. 1271)
**B. Review contributing medications, hydration status, and reversible kidney dysfunction.** Correct, this follows the source’s outpatient approach by addressing drugs, hydration, and reversible causes of reduced kidney function. (p. 1271)
**C. Give intravenous calcium to remove the excess potassium from the body.** Wrong, calcium stabilizes the myocardial membrane; the source explicitly states that this effect does not lower potassium levels. (p. 1271)
**D. Give sodium bicarbonate while deferring assessment of acid-base status.** Wrong, the source conditions bicarbonate use on accompanying metabolic acidosis, so deferring acid-base assessment misses that condition. (p. 1271)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 1271.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: A patient with chronic kidney disease takes spironolactone and develops non-life-threatening hyperkalemia. Which approach addresses a reversible contributor to the potassium elevation?
o: Add another inhibitor of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
Identify and stop a medication contributing to hyperkalemia
Add a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug to improve clearance
Continue the medication and defer evaluation until ECG changes appear
explanation:
**Medication review** is part of treating non-life-threatening hyperkalemia. Hazzard includes "elimination of medications that cause hyperkalemia" in management and warns that a normal ECG does not make potassium elevation insignificant (p. 1271).

**A. Add another inhibitor of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.** Wrong, using two inhibitors of this system is listed among high-risk situations for severe hyperkalemia (p. 1271).
**B. Identify and stop a medication contributing to hyperkalemia.** Correct, removing a contributing medication addresses a reversible factor explicitly identified in the treatment approach (p. 1271).
**C. Add a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug to improve clearance.** Wrong, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are listed among high-risk situations for severe hyperkalemia, not as a means of correcting it (p. 1271).
**D. Continue the medication and defer evaluation until ECG changes appear.** Wrong, absence of ECG changes does not establish that hyperkalemia is insignificant and does not justify postponing review of reversible causes (p. 1271).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1271.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: A patient with chronic kidney disease requests treatment for joint pain. Which prescribing principle is emphasized in Hazzard’s chapter on the aging kidney?
o: Prefer NSAIDs as a means of preserving the patient’s residual kidney function
Choose medication doses without accounting for the extent of renal excretion
Avoid potential renal toxins and adjust renally excreted medication dosing
Choose dosing intervals without accounting for the extent of renal excretion
explanation:
**Preserving residual kidney function** includes avoiding potential renal toxins and accounting for renal excretion when prescribing. Hazzard identifies NSAIDs among the potential toxins and states: "Medications excreted by the kidney should be appropriately dosed in amount and frequency." (p. 1275).

**A. Prefer NSAIDs as a means of preserving the patient’s residual kidney function.** Wrong, NSAIDs are listed as potential renal toxins to avoid, rather than as drugs used to preserve kidney function (p. 1275).
**B. Choose medication doses without accounting for the extent of renal excretion.** Wrong, the amount prescribed must be appropriate for a drug excreted by the kidney; disregarding renal excretion omits that adjustment (p. 1275).
**C. Avoid potential renal toxins and adjust renally excreted medication dosing.** Correct, this combines the two medication principles stated for patients with impaired kidney function (p. 1275).
**D. Choose dosing intervals without accounting for the extent of renal excretion.** Wrong, frequency, as well as dose amount, requires adjustment for medications excreted by the kidney (p. 1275).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1275.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: An older woman with reduced renal clearance is taking a medication excreted by the kidney. Which principle should guide a safety review of the prescription?
o: Consider increasing the dose to compensate for reduced kidney function.
Consider adjusting the dose amount and the frequency of administration.
Consider shortening dose intervals to compensate for reduced renal clearance.
Consider adjusting for the clinical response while disregarding renal clearance.
explanation:
For drugs **excreted by the kidney**, Hazzard recommends appropriate dosing in both **amount and frequency** when kidney function is impaired (p. 1275). Elimination of many drugs occurs through renal clearance, so renal-based individualized dosing is relevant to the prescription review (p. 303).
"Medications excreted by the kidney should be appropriately dosed in amount and frequency." (p. 1275).

**A. Consider increasing the dose to compensate for reduced kidney function.** Wrong, renal clearance is a route of drug elimination. Increasing the dose merely because clearance has fallen does not follow the recommendation for individualized renal dosing (inference, pp. 303, 1275).
**B. Consider adjusting the dose amount and the frequency of administration.** Correct, both the amount per dose and how often it is given are explicitly named in the source recommendation (p. 1275).
**C. Consider shortening dose intervals to compensate for reduced renal clearance.** Wrong, renal clearance contributes to elimination. Shortening intervals to compensate for reduced clearance increases administration rather than adapting it to reduced elimination (inference, pp. 303, 1275).
**D. Consider adjusting for the clinical response while disregarding renal clearance.** Wrong, the source describes renal-based dosing of renally cleared drugs; disregarding clearance excludes a stated basis for individualizing the prescription (pp. 303, 1275).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 303, 1275.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: An 80-year-old man with renal failure and severe hyperkalemia develops a conduction abnormality on ECG. Which treatment provides immediate myocardial protection by stabilizing the cell membrane while potassium-lowering treatment is also planned?
o: Administer intravenous calcium gluconate
Administer insulin by the intravenous route
Administer an intravenous loop diuretic
Administer an oral ion-exchange resin
explanation:
**Intravenous calcium gluconate** stabilizes the myocardial cell membrane in severe hyperkalemia with cardiac effects. Its action is immediate but transient and does not lower potassium, so treatment must also address potassium redistribution and removal as appropriate (p. 1271). "Intravenous calcium gluconate will stabilize the myocardial cell membrane, decreasing the potential for cardiac arrest." (p. 1271).

**A. Administer intravenous calcium gluconate.** Correct, this is the intervention identified as providing immediate myocardial membrane stabilization, the mechanism asked for in the stem (p. 1271).
**B. Administer insulin by the intravenous route.** Wrong, insulin promotes potassium entry into cells; that lowers serum potassium rather than supplying the direct membrane-stabilizing action asked for (p. 1271).
**C. Administer an intravenous loop diuretic.** Wrong, loop-diuretic therapy is listed among methods for removing potassium from the body, rather than immediate myocardial membrane stabilization (p. 1271).
**D. Administer an oral ion-exchange resin.** Wrong, exchange resins are listed as potassium-removal therapy, rather than the immediate myocardial protection provided by calcium (p. 1271).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1271.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: An 81-year-old man has severe hyperkalemia with bradycardia and marked conduction delay. What immediate effect does Hazzard attribute to intravenous calcium gluconate in this situation?
o: An immediate increase in urinary potassium loss through enhanced excretion by the kidneys.
An immediate redistribution of extracellular potassium into cells through increased cellular potassium uptake.
An immediate reduction in body potassium stores through enhanced intestinal elimination of potassium.
An immediate stabilization of myocardial cell membranes with a transient reduction in cardiac risk.
explanation:
In severe hyperkalemia with cardiac effects, **intravenous calcium gluconate** stabilizes the myocardial cell membrane and decreases the potential for cardiac arrest (p. 1271). It provides immediate but transient protection rather than lowering the potassium level; shifting potassium into cells and removing potassium from the body are distinct treatment effects. "This effect is essentially immediate, but transient, and does not lower potassium levels." (p. 1271).

**A. An immediate increase in urinary potassium loss through enhanced excretion by the kidneys.** Wrong, renal elimination removes potassium from the body, whereas calcium’s immediate action is membrane stabilization without potassium reduction. The source separately describes forced diuresis among potassium-removal measures (p. 1271).
**B. An immediate redistribution of extracellular potassium into cells through increased cellular potassium uptake.** Wrong, intracellular shifting lowers serum potassium and is attributed to insulin, inhaled beta-agonists, and bicarbonate in the setting of metabolic acidosis. Calcium is described as stabilizing the myocardial membrane without lowering potassium (p. 1271).
**C. An immediate reduction in body potassium stores through enhanced intestinal elimination of potassium.** Wrong, intestinal exchange belongs to potassium-removal treatment. Calcium does not remove potassium or lower its concentration; the source separates its immediate membrane effect from removal measures such as exchange resins (p. 1271).
**D. An immediate stabilization of myocardial cell membranes with a transient reduction in cardiac risk.** Correct, the bradycardia and conduction delay match the source’s description of severe hyperkalemia requiring immediate intervention. Calcium stabilizes the myocardial membrane, with an immediate but transient effect and no reduction in potassium level (p. 1271).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1271.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: An older adult taking spironolactone starts trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Which electrolyte risk does Hazzard emphasize for this combination?
o: Development of significant hyperkalemia during treatment
Development of hypokalemia from the combined medications
A sustained potassium decrease requiring preventive supplementation
Potassium loss that offsets the effect of spironolactone
explanation:
**Hyperkalemia** can reflect reduced kidney function together with medications that impair potassium handling. Hazzard specifically identifies trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in a patient taking spironolactone as a high-risk situation for severe hyperkalemia (p. 1271). The listed combination is "the use of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole in patients on spironolactone" (p. 1271).

**A. Development of significant hyperkalemia during treatment.** Correct, the source explicitly identifies this drug combination among high-risk situations for severe hyperkalemia (p. 1271).
**B. Development of hypokalemia from the combined medications.** Wrong, the named risk is potassium elevation, not potassium depletion from the combination (p. 1271).
**C. A sustained potassium decrease requiring preventive supplementation.** Wrong, the source identifies a risk of potassium elevation; a preventive potassium supplement does not address that risk (p. 1271).
**D. Potassium loss that offsets the effect of spironolactone.** Wrong, the combination is described as a high-risk setting for severe hyperkalemia, not a compensating potassium-losing interaction (p. 1271).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1271.
ref: Hazzard Ch 82 — AGING OF THE KIDNEY

q: Why can a rising serum creatinine be pathological even when it remains near the laboratory normal range?
o: A value at the upper limit of normal excludes significant loss of renal function
Serum creatinine should rise with normal aging and need not affect renal drug dosing
Creatinine production increases as muscle mass falls, so a rising level is normal aging
Muscle loss reduces creatinine production, so serum creatinine should remain relatively constant
explanation:
Loss of muscle mass reduces creatinine production, so serum creatinine should remain relatively constant and an upper-normal level can reflect important renal decline (p1268).

C. Creatinine production increases as muscle mass falls, so a rising level is normal aging: The book describes reduced creatinine production with loss of muscle mass (p1268).
A. A value at the upper limit of normal excludes significant loss of renal function: The book states that an upper-normal level can represent significant decline in an older individual (p1268).
B. Serum creatinine should rise with normal aging and need not affect renal drug dosing: The book says creatinine should remain relatively constant and elevations warrant attention to renal function and dosing (p1268).

q: Is proteinuria an expected consequence of normal human aging?
o: No - proteinuria is pathological and requires a full work-up in older humans
No - proteinuria needs no work-up when creatinine stays in its normal range
Yes - the normal decline in GFR makes proteinuria expected in older humans
Yes - proteinuria is normal in aging humans as it is in rats
explanation:
**Proteinuria is not normal human kidney aging**, even though GFR declines with age. Hazzard requires a full work-up and explicitly distinguishes humans from rodent models, in which proteinuria is a normal aging feature (p. 1269).
"Proteinuria is always a pathological finding and requires a full work-up." (p. 1269).

**A. No - proteinuria is pathological and requires a full work-up in older humans.** Correct, proteinuria is a pathological finding in an older human and warrants investigation rather than attribution to age (p. 1269).
**B. No - proteinuria needs no work-up when creatinine stays in its normal range.** Wrong, preserved filtration does not exclude kidney damage: the source recognizes proteinuria with preserved GFR and still requires a full work-up (p. 1269).
**C. Yes - the normal decline in GFR makes proteinuria expected in older humans.** Wrong, age-related GFR decline and proteinuria are not equivalent; the source specifically says proteinuria is not normal despite the decline in GFR (p. 1269).
**D. Yes - proteinuria is normal in aging humans as it is in rats.** Wrong, the rat finding does not transfer to humans, for whom the same passage classifies proteinuria as pathological (p. 1269).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1269.

q: As GFR declines, how does potassium fractional excretion differ in older versus younger adults?
o: The fractional excretion of potassium does not rise as much as in young individuals
It rises more than in young individuals because aldosterone levels increase
A smaller fractional-excretion rise usually makes unstressed serum potassium abnormal
The fractional-excretion rise is similar in younger and older adults despite declining GFR
explanation:
As kidney filtration falls, **older adults have a smaller compensatory rise in fractional potassium excretion** than younger adults. The chapter attributes this partly to lower aldosterone levels or aldosterone resistance, while noting that potassium may remain normal under unstressed conditions when kidney function is relatively preserved (p. 1270).
"the fractional excretion of potassium does not rise as much as in young individuals" (p. 1270).

**A. The fractional excretion of potassium does not rise as much as in young individuals.** Correct, this is the reduced adaptive response described as GFR declines in older adults (p. 1270).
**B. It rises more than in young individuals because aldosterone levels increase.** Wrong, the source describes lower aldosterone activity or resistance and a smaller increase in fractional excretion, not an enhanced response driven by higher aldosterone (p. 1270).
**C. A smaller fractional-excretion rise usually makes unstressed serum potassium abnormal.** Wrong, a reduced reserve does not imply that baseline potassium must be abnormal; the source describes normal unstressed potassium with relatively preserved kidney function (p. 1270).
**D. The fractional-excretion rise is similar in younger and older adults despite declining GFR.** Wrong, the responses are not equivalent: older adults increase fractional potassium excretion less as GFR falls (p. 1270).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1270.

q: Does absence of typical ECG changes exclude dangerous hyperkalemia?
o: No - absence of ECG findings does not make hyperkalemia erroneous or insignificant
No - a given potassium level usually produces the same ECG pattern across patients
Yes - the classic sequence of ECG changes is the usual pattern of dangerous hyperkalemia
Yes - an absent ECG pattern generally establishes that the potassium result is erroneous
explanation:
**A normal-looking ECG does not exclude important hyperkalemia**. Cardiac effects can be subtle, and the same potassium level can produce very different ECG findings, so the familiar sequence of progressively abnormal waves is seldom seen in practice (p1271). Absence of that pattern cannot establish that the measured potassium is spurious or harmless (p1271).
"the same level of hyperkalemia may produce vastly different effects on the electrocardiogram (ECG)" (p1271).

**A. No - absence of ECG findings does not make hyperkalemia erroneous or insignificant.** Correct, this preserves the need to take a high potassium result seriously despite absent typical ECG findings (p1271).
**B. No - a given potassium level usually produces the same ECG pattern across patients.** Wrong, the conclusion starts correctly, but its explanation is wrong: a given potassium level can produce widely different ECG effects across patients (p1271).
**C. Yes - the classic sequence of ECG changes is the usual pattern of dangerous hyperkalemia.** Wrong, this relies on a stereotyped progression that the source says is seldom seen, so it cannot safely exclude dangerous hyperkalemia (p1271).
**D. Yes - an absent ECG pattern generally establishes that the potassium result is erroneous.** Wrong, absence of ECG findings is not evidence that the laboratory result is erroneous; the source explicitly warns against this conclusion (p1271).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p1271.

q: What makes podocyte loss important in the proposed sclerosis mechanism?
o: Damaged podocytes are postmitotic cells without the capacity for replacement
Complete glomerular sclerosis preserves the affected nephron and its filtration capacity
Podocyte detachment maintains basement-membrane coverage and protects against glomerular sclerosis
Podocytes multiply in proportion to the enlargement of the glomerular tuft
explanation:
**Podocyte loss** matters because these postmitotic cells are not replaced after damage. In the proposed mechanism, tuft enlargement leaves podocytes covering an increasing area; detachment exposes basement membrane and initiates sclerosis, eventually costing the affected nephron its filtration capacity (p. 1272).
"These specialized cells are postmitotic and if damaged in any way, cannot be replaced." (p. 1272).

**A. Damaged podocytes are postmitotic cells without the capacity for replacement.** Correct, loss persists because these cells lack replacement capacity, making their depletion important in the proposed sclerosis mechanism (p. 1272).
**B. Complete glomerular sclerosis preserves the affected nephron and its filtration capacity.** Wrong, complete sclerosis causes the glomerulus to shrivel with loss of the nephron and its filtration capacity, rather than preserving them (p. 1272).
**C. Podocyte detachment maintains basement-membrane coverage and protects against glomerular sclerosis.** Wrong, detachment leaves bare basement membrane, which the proposed mechanism identifies as a trigger for sclerosis (p. 1272).
**D. Podocytes multiply in proportion to the enlargement of the glomerular tuft.** Wrong, postmitotic podocytes do not multiply to match the expanding tuft, unlike the increase in endothelial and mesangial cells described on this page (p. 1272).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1272.

q: Does the chapter establish protein restriction as prevention of normal human kidney aging?
o: No - protein restriction tends to worsen symptoms in established uremia
Yes - lower-protein vegetarians had better-preserved kidney function than meat eaters
Yes - animal studies establish prevention of normal human kidney aging
No - evidence supports uremic symptom reduction, not prevention of human kidney aging
explanation:
**Symptom management in established kidney disease** is different from prevention of normal kidney aging (p. 1274). Protein restriction can reduce uremic symptoms, but animal findings do not establish human prevention: “The relevance of these studies in humans remains unclear.” (p. 1274).

**A. No - protein restriction tends to worsen symptoms in established uremia.** Wrong, the source supports reduction, not worsening, of uremic symptoms in established renal disease (p. 1274).
**B. Yes - lower-protein vegetarians had better-preserved kidney function than meat eaters.** Wrong, the cited vegetarian and nonvegetarian groups had no difference in kidney function, so they do not establish preservation by protein restriction (p. 1274).
**C. Yes - animal studies establish prevention of normal human kidney aging.** Wrong, the chapter explicitly says the relevance of the animal studies to humans is unclear; extrapolation does not establish prevention (p. 1274).
**D. No - evidence supports uremic symptom reduction, not prevention of human kidney aging.** Correct, this preserves the distinction between the supported symptomatic use and the unsupported claim of preventing age-related human kidney changes (p. 1274).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1274.
